Born in 1993 in Surabaya, IDN. Father, 31 at the child's birth, grew up in dense, humid Javanese streets where neighbors always watched but rarely intervened, learning early that it was safer to smooth tension than to confront it. Outwardly he is easygoing and quick with a small joke, but that humor mostly bends back on himself; anger at bosses, officials, and fate is swallowed and turned into longer hours and quiet smoking breaks. His religiosity is steady but untheatrical—Friday prayers, muttered du‘a on the angkot, a vague fear that he is not doing enough which he manages by working rather than talking. At home he is the softer parent, the one who buys snacks and fixes broken things, yet he often drifts into TV or his workshop when emotions rise, convinced that his presence doesn’t really change the deeper currents. Approaching fatherhood, he hopes the baby will “have more choices” and “not be stepped on” the way he feels he has been, but he has no clear plan beyond trying to be a little kinder and less explosive than the men who raised him.
Father, 31 at the child's birth, grew up in dense, noisy Javanese streets where everyone watched but few intervened, learning early that it was safer to smooth things over than push back. He presents as understated and gentle, with a habit of turning jokes against himself when conflict brushes too close, but there is a slow, pressurized annoyance at bosses, officials, and fate that rarely finds words. His religiosity is steady but unshowy: Friday prayers, small muttered du‘a on the angkot, and a private anxiety that he isn’t doing enough for God or his family, which he manages by working longer hours rather than talking. In the household he is the easy parent, the one who buys snacks and fixes broken toys, but he also disappears into the workshop or TV when emotions run hot, carrying an unspoken conviction that his presence doesn’t really change outcomes. As a parent-to-be he hopes the baby will “have more choices” and “not be stepped on,” but he cannot yet imagine how to model that; his default defense is to absorb pressure quietly and teach the child, by example, to bend rather than break. Mother, 20 at the child's birth, grew up in a crowded Banten neighborhood where survival meant pushing back first and apologizing later, and she learned quickly that softness was something other people got punished for. Her warmth runs hot and fast—she will laugh loudly, shove a plate of food into your hands, and argue on your behalf with a shopkeeper—but it is wrapped in a hard shell of authority: doors are slammed, orders barked, and apologies rare. Underneath, she carries a deep file of betrayals and disappointments from men and kin who did not protect her, so her default defense is to control whatever she can: the timing of meals, the way money is spent, who talks to whom. Religion is both anchor and armor; she throws herself into prayer and ritual but also uses moral language like a blade, insisting on strength and self-reliance as signs of faith. As a parent-to-be she is both fiercely determined and quietly afraid—vowing that no one will ever walk over her child the way people have walked over her, but also half-convinced that the only way to keep a baby safe is to make them tough early, even if that means they never see her flinch.
Mother, 30 at the child's birth, grew up in the same crowded urban lanes but learned a different survival script: stay useful, stay kind, and people will keep you close. She moves through family and neighborhood with quick, anticipatory warmth—topping up tea before anyone asks, remembering who likes which sambal—but there’s a tightness in her shoulders when she’s alone, a fear that if she ever stopped giving, she would simply be left behind. Her religiosity is more visible than her husband’s: headscarf pinned just so, regular women’s study circles, a constant low-grade anxiety about whether she is raising “good” children in a world that feels looser and less predictable than her own youth. Authority at home comes out as fussing and moral reminders rather than direct commands; when angry she over-functions—cleaning harder, cooking more—rather than resting or stating what she wants. As a parent-to-be she is already rehearsing sacrifices she hasn’t been asked for, half-resentful and half-proud, imagining a child who will be both dutiful and more confident than she has ever dared to be herself.
